extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York and readers interested in constitutional design, federalism, and controlling faction (general public and political theorists)
extracted.subtask_short: federalist arguments on union and faction
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize the constitutional and political criteria advanced in Federalist Papers Nos. IX–XI (Madison and Hamilton) concerning the design and effects of a federal union: controlling faction, the character of a confederate republic, commercial policy, and naval power. Targets readers evaluating the merits of a united national government versus disunion or smaller republics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and flexibility of a confederate republic
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of a CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC seems simply to be 'an assemblage of societies,' or an association of two or more states into one state. The extent, modifications, and objects of the federal authority are mere matters of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: So long as the separate organization of the members be not abolished; so long as it exists, by a constitutional necessity, for local purposes; though it should be in perfect subordination to the general authority of the union, it would still be, in fact and in theory, an association of states, or a confederacy. Example: Lycian confederacy gave the common council appointment of local judges, yet Montesquieu praised it; thus the precise limits of federal interference are discretionary and not fixed by an abstract distinction between 'confederacy' and 'consolidation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Union as a safeguard against domestic faction and insurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the numerous advantages promised by a well-constructed Union, none deserves to be more accurately developed than its tendency to break and control the violence of faction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison argues the Union reduces instability, injustice, and confusion in public councils by making factious combinations less dangerous and less able to execute schemes of oppression. The Union's larger sphere and representative institutions are key mechanisms in this safeguard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two general methods to cure the mischiefs of faction
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two methods of curing the mischiefs of faction: the one, by removing its causes; the other, by controlling its effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing causes would require either destroying liberty or making everyone have the same opinions/interests—both impractical or undesirable. Therefore, controlling effects (structural remedies) is the feasible path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticality and unacceptability of removing faction's causes
rubrics_metrics.description: There are again two methods of removing the causes of faction: the one, by destroying the liberty which is essential to its existence; the other, by giving to every citizen the same opinions, the same passions, and the same interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison rejects both: destroying liberty is worse than the disease; making all opinions/interests identical is impossible because reason is fallible and human faculties/interests differ (especially property). Thus institutional design must accept factional causes as inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republican representation and a larger sphere control factional effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic—delegating government to a small number of citizens elected by the rest and extended over a greater number of citizens and territory—opens a different prospect and promises the cure sought for faction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two key differences from a pure democracy: (1) representation 'refines and enlarges the public views' by filtering through chosen representatives; (2) a greater number of citizens and larger territory increases variety of parties/interests, making it less probable that a majority will form a common motive to oppress others. Thus a large republic (or Union) is preferable to a small one or to direct democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative selection improved by larger republic scale (but requires balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a large republic the proportion of fit characters may be as great or greater, and representatives chosen by a greater number of citizens will be less subject to the 'vicious arts' that carry elections in small polities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison notes a mean is necessary: too large an electorate makes representatives unfamiliar with local circumstances; too small renders them unduly attached to local interests. The federal Constitution combines national and state legislatures to balance aggregate and local interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing majority tyranny by preventing coexistent passions or frustrating concert
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the existence of the same passion or interest in a majority at the same time must be prevented, or the majority, having such coexistent passion or interest, must be rendered, by their number and local situation, unable to concert and carry into effect schemes of oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural remedies include extending the sphere (more varied interests) so that common motives are unlikely, and making communication/coordination across wide territory and many groups more difficult, thus hindering the formation and execution of oppressive majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislators must not be judges in their own causes; institutional separation needed
rubrics_metrics.description: No man is allowed to be a judge in his own cause, because his interest would certainly bias his judgment... With equal, nay with greater reason, a body of men are unfit to be both judges and parties at the same time; yet what are many of the most important acts of legislation, but so many judicial determinations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because legislators are parties to interests (creditors vs debtors, landed vs manufacturing), institutional arrangements (representation, larger electorate, checks) are necessary to mitigate the temptation for majorities to trample on rights for their own benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union strengthens commercial negotiation and reduces foreign leverage
rubrics_metrics.description: By prohibitory regulations, extending, at the same time, throughout the States, we may oblige foreign countries to bid against each other, for the privileges of our markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A united market of millions increases bargaining power with European powers; coordinated prohibitions or trade policy can induce foreign governments to concede privileges (example: hypothetical exclusion of Great Britain). Disunion would allow foreign powers to intermediate trade (via Dutch) and capture shipping/profits, reducing American advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union enables creation and sustainment of a national navy
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal navy... would embrace the resources of all [states]; a navy of the United States is an object far less remote than a navy of any single State or partial confederacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union concentrates naval stores (tar, pitch, turpentine), shipbuilding timber (South), iron (Middle/Southern), and seamen (North), making a national navy feasible and effective—crucial for protecting commerce, asserting rights (West Indies operations), and raising the nation's diplomatic weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union secures collective maritime and territorial rights (fisheries, navigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are rights of great moment to the trade of America which are rights of the Union—I allude to the fisheries, to the navigation of the Western lakes, and to that of the Mississippi. The dissolution of the Confederacy would give room for delicate questions concerning the future existence of these rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If states disunite, more powerful partners (foreign powers) would likely resolve such questions to American disadvantage (e.g., Spain and the Mississippi), whereas a united national government protects these collective interests and the economic benefits that flow from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disunion risks passive commerce and external domination
rubrics_metrics.description: In a state of disunion... our commerce would be a prey to the wanton intermeddlings of all nations at war with each other... We should then be compelled to content ourselves with the first price of our commodities, and to see the profits of our trade snatched from us to enrich our enemies and persecutors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disunion would make the U.S. politically and commercially weak—vulnerable to depredations, deprived of the rights of neutrality unless defended by adequate power, and subject to foreign manipulation that would stifle American commerce, navigation, and maritime enterprise.
